metaData.originalTitle: 700 亿元狂飙的失控产业背后：谁在收割一代焦虑家长？
metaData.title: Behind the 70 Billion Yuan Runaway Uncontrolled Industry: Who Is Preying on a Generation of Anxious Parents?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Through firsthand accounts from multiple affected students, parents, and industry insiders, this article deeply exposes the industrial chain of closed institutions operating under the guise of internet addiction treatment and rebellion correction, revealing how violent punishment, psychological manipulation, and profiteering models exploit parental anxiety to prey on families.
metaData.summary: This article is an in-depth investigative report from Sanlian Life Weekly. Through interviews with multiple teenagers who were sent to internet addiction treatment or special training institutions in Henan and other places, their parents, former instructors, psychological counselors, and scholars, it comprehensively reveals the dark side of the 'juvenile behavioral correction' industry with annual revenue exceeding 70 billion yuan. The article starts with specific cases—14-year-old Wu Rong was tricked by her parents into 'Lixuan Education' under the pretext of a police investigation, where she underwent 540 days of military-style management and ruler-based corporal punishment; 13-year-old Liu Jiahao suffered physical abuse at the 'Yashengsi Quality Education Base', including running with a tire around his body. The report traces the evolution of the industry: from Yang Yongxin's electroshock therapy to traditional Chinese studies academies and special training camps, and to the current form of education consulting companies and family education courses that attract customers through short-video platforms. Parents, anxious about their children's school aversion, rebelliousness, and gaming addiction, pay high fees (30,000 to 50,000 yuan per year) for 'quick correction' services, but the institutions often respond with violence, brainwashing, and fabricated videos. Scholars and lawyers point out that these institutions generally lack proper qualifications for education, medical care, and accommodation, and supervision is severely lacking. Many victims say such experiences leave long-term psychological trauma and further deteriorate their relationship with their parents, but parents are often unaware of this.

mainPoints.point: Closed behavioral correction institutions employ violent punishment and psychological control as core methods.
mainPoints.explanation: Students often suffer physical punishment such as being beaten with rulers, forced to run, made to kneel with a tire around them, or other forms of corporal punishment for behaviors like talking back or stealing cigarettes; instructors can arbitrarily inflict violence. The institutions create the illusion of reform by isolating communication, enforcing gratitude brainwashing, and staging videos.

mainPoints.point: Parental anxiety is precisely harvested by businesses, forming a gray industry with annual revenue exceeding 70 billion yuan.
mainPoints.explanation: Parents, driven by their children's problems such as school aversion, gaming addiction, and rebelliousness, and lacking effective channels for help, are attracted by the institutions' promises of 'quick correction' and staged videos, paying tuition fees ranging from 30,000 to 100,000 yuan per year. The industry's profit margins exceed 100%.

mainPoints.point: The industry's form evolves with public opinion and platforms, but its core remains unchanged—exploiting social anxiety.
mainPoints.explanation: From electroshock therapy to traditional Chinese studies academies, and then to education consulting companies on short-video platforms, the model continuously changes its name and appearance, but it is always built on parents' worries about their uncontrollable children and their expectations of 'quick correction'.

mainPoints.point: There is a severe lack of regulation; most institutions have no compliance qualifications and operate transiently.
mainPoints.explanation: These institutions need to obtain licenses from multiple departments—education, civil affairs, and health—but in reality, most operate solely on a business license. Once reported or exposed, they move and rename, even restricting parents' visits.

keyQuotes: From the early internet addiction treatments characterized by electroshock, to later closed correctional institutions named 'traditional Chinese studies academies' and 'special training camps', and now to various institutions appearing in the forms of 'education consulting companies' and 'family education courses', this system continuously changes its external packaging and operational discourse, but its core remains unchanged—it is always built on the same social anxiety: concerns about out-of-control adolescents and even adults, and the expectation of 'quick correction'.

relatedArticles.title: The Death of a 30-Year-Old Shanghai Kindergarten Teacher Amidst Parent Complaint Disputes
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Wang Peng, a 30-year-old kindergarten teacher in Shanghai, fell into deep anxiety due to disputes involving parent complaints and ultimately drowned; the report reveals the tension in school-parent relationships and the professional pressure on kindergarten teachers through interviews with family, colleagues, and parents.

relatedArticles.title: Blue Origin's Explosion Was More Than Just a Rocket
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket exploded during a static fire test, destroying its only launch pad and rendering it unable to launch for the next two to three years, severely impacting its own business, NASA's lunar plans, Amazon's satellite deployment, and highlighting SpaceX's monopoly in commercial spaceflight.

relatedArticles.title: Young People Who Can't Make Friends with Colleagues: Too Hurt by the Fierce Job Race?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Yuan Changgeng, an associate professor of sociology at Yunnan University, analyzes the changing perceptions of work meaning among young people from a historical perspective, pointing out that workplace difficulties stem from the mismatch between modern professional environments and personal expectations, and emphasizing the possibility of rebuilding work value through daily life and interpersonal connections.

relatedArticles.title: A Rural Sister's 30-Year Pursuit of Justice for Her Late Brother
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This is the true story of Li Haiyu, who, after her younger brother was murdered, spent thirty years in a grueling pursuit of justice, eventually bringing the killer to account through her own relentless efforts, demonstrating extraordinary resilience and persistence.

relatedArticles.title: After the Silence: Frank Wang and DJI's 'System Reboot' Moment
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the twenty-year journey of DJI founder Frank Wang, from a technically obsessive engineer to a systems manager, revealing the company's transformation from being technology-driven, through organizational growing pains, to ultimately embracing capability orientation and systemic self-consistency.

relatedArticles.title: A Film Smearing Altman, Shelved Overnight by OpenAI's Biggest Backer
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Amazon MGM pulled the film 'Artificial' about OpenAI's internal strife, due to Amazon's huge cooperation with OpenAI, making the film's negative portrayal of Altman a commercial risk, reflecting the invisible intervention of tech capital on narratives.

relatedArticles.title: A Trafficked Woman and the Bigamy Conviction She Has Carried for 37 Years
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article reports the case of Guo Xiaoling, a trafficked woman who was sold to a buyer in Shandong 37 years ago and subsequently married the buyer, only to be prosecuted for bigamy by her husband and sentenced to prison, leading to a long-term but unsuccessful appeal process that reveals the complex judicial predicament faced by trafficking victims.

relatedArticles.title: The New Global 'Middle-Class Darling': Why Is It Mass-Produced in China?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores the 'Embodied AI' wave, analyzing how China leverages its robust supply chain clusters, manufacturing speed, and application deployment capabilities to demonstrate a global competitive advantage and explore new business models in AI hardware (e.g., AI toys, smart wearables).

relatedArticles.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Microsoft Build 2026: The 'Agent-First' Era Arrives with Seven In-House Models
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Microsoft Build 2026 unveiled seven in-house MAI models, the Scout agent, the MXC system-level security sandbox, and Project Solara, marking the full implementation of an 'Agent-First' strategy.

relatedArticles.title: After Abundance: AI Coding Observation Report 2.0｜AI Lens Series
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Tencent Research Institute releases the "AI Coding Observation Report 2.0," which reviews 7 non-consensus judgments and extracts 6 structural insights including model convergence, Agent-native approaches, verification bottlenecks, scarcity of taste, SaaS restructuring, and redefinition of developers. It points out that AI Coding is transitioning from a "battlefield of prior beliefs" to a state "after abundance," where scarce capabilities have shifted from code generation to taste, judgment, and engineering discipline.
